newsitem.title: Afghanistan: Taleban reject U.N. call for Afghan ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Taleban reject U.N. call for Afghan ceasefire.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban rulers rejected on Thursday calls by U.N. special envoy Norbert Holl for a ceasefire, saying they would not lay down their weapons until all Afghans had been disarmed.
Earlier on Thursday Holl told Reuters he was meeting Taleban officials and planned to meet those of other factions, to call for a ceasefire after heavy fighting broke out north of Kabul.

"It is useless to observe a ceasefire with those who stress fighting and as you know in Bagram and these areas we have not collected the weapons and we have left the people alone," acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told a news conference.
"But they have started an insurgency and a ceasefire with these people is not important.
"If they give up their insurgency and give up their government property there is no need actually for a ceasefire because we don't have any fight with them."
The Taleban appeared to have suffered further reverses at the hands of ousted military chief Ahmad Shah Masood on Thursday as a town south of previous fighting prepared to defend itself.

"There are heavy casualties among soldiers but also among innocent civilians. At a moment like this, the United Nations cannot sit on the fence," Holl said after meeting Taleban officials at Kabul's foreign ministry.

"We have to stand up and this is part of my peace mission and I have to talk to the parties. This is why I have come to see the Taleban and you may jump to the conclusion that I will also see other parties. The most important matter now is to come to a ceasefire,"
He did not elaborate.
Holl has been shuttling between factions for the past two weeks in a desperate attempt to stop another round of civil war in the ravaged country.

But the Taleban's Mutaqi said that reports of fighting and serious losses were "baseless", adding that the Taleban still held the area south of the Salang tunnel, Jabal-os-Saraj and Golbahar, the town at the entrance to the Panjsher valley.

According to travellers, the area has been the scene of fierce fighting in the past 48 hours, with Taleban fighters suspending an assault on Masood's Panjsher stronghold to defend positions north of the town of Jabal-os-Saraj to the west.

The area marks the meeting point between the main plain north of Kabul and the Hindu Kush, a vast mountain range providing natural defences for both Masood and warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum, who has yet to openly commit to either side.
It has been the first serious reverse in months for the Taleban, which swept the capital and surrounding areas in a lightning campaign last month.

"The news that the Taleban has sustained huge losses is completely baseless. The number of the losses is about 10, and two of them who were trapped and arrested by the enemy and later burned alive...at the entrance to Panjsher valley," Mutaqi said.
Aid workers, travellers and local people said they had seen many Taleban bodies and wounded being ferried from the area.
Mutaqi conceded there had been a revolt in Bagram, a small town near the military airbase of the same name, but he said it had been quelled.
"Some people misused the good morals of the Taleban in these areas. They had launched attacks against the Taleban and some of them were arrested during the fighting," he said.
"Anyone who acts against the will and the wishes of the people of Afghanistan are the enemies of Afghanistan and we will punish them."
Masood, his political mentor deposed president Burhanuddin Rabbani and Dostum were due to hold talks in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif on Thursday.
The Taleban has been anxious to avoid provoking Dostum into joining forces with other rival factions for fear of facing well-armed and trained armies on two fronts.
